newsitem.title: RWANDA: Zaire rebels ponder next move after victories.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels ponder next move after victories.

text.p: A Zairean rebel group has scored stunning military advances in eastern Zaire but now appears divided on what to do next, analysts said on Wednesday.
They said some in the rebel camp were pushing for further military action against Zaire's army while others sought a mediated political settlement.

To address diverse opinions in Africa's latest rebel group, the leadership called a three-week unilateral ceasefire from November 4, ostensibly to allow trapped Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees to return to their homelands.

But rebel insiders say the three-week period was to enable strategists in the Democratic Alliance of Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) to return to the drawing board to plot the next move in Africa's newest war.
"They are back at the drawing board. They have to think and think hard about where they go next," an African ambassador with close connections to the rebel leadership told Reuters.
"They have two clear options: to pursue military activity at the risk of attracting international intervention or open dialogue with Kinshasa," he said.

On Tuesday, eight African countries met in the Kenyan capital Nairobi and urged the United Nations to arrange a "neutral" protection force to come to the rescue of a million abandoned Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees trapped and scattered by the Zaire fighting.
War in the east began when the Banyamulenge, an ethnic Tutsi community of about 400,000, resisted Zairean attempts to expel them to Rwanda, a land their ancestors left up to 200 years ago.
Within a week of organising armed resistance, the Banyamulenge were quickly joined by other forces opposed to Zairean leader Mobutu Sese Seko's autocratic rule.
For 30 years Mobutu has ruled his sprawling, potentially rich Central African nation as a personal fiefdom.

But Mobutu, who has kept the country together using a mixture of state brutality, cunning and bribery, is ailing in Europe and there are people in the rebel camp who wish to capitalise on his absence to break up the country.
Zaire's army and its transitional government are trading accusations and anti-Tutsi riots have shaken the capital Kinshasa, 1,600 km (1,000 miles) west of the fighting zone.

"Some (rebel) commanders are openly calling for secession from the rest of Zaire. This thinking rests on the premise that taking on the broader Zaire would bog down the ADFL and arouse sympathy for Kinshasa," a Rwandan military strategist said.

But Organisation of African Unity (OAU) representative to the Great Lakes region, Joe Felli, told Reuters: "The OAU will not allow Zaire to break up into units. The territorial integrity of Zaire is paramount and non-negotiable."
Analysts said Rwanda's final word on the Zairean conflict would have much more bearing on what the ADFL did next.

Zaire is host to more than a million Rwandan Hutu refugees and a 45,000-strong former Rwandan Hutu army ousted by Kigali's current rulers in 1994. Many are blamed for the 1994 genocide of a million Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus.
The presence of the Hutus in a region where ethnic Tutsis have lived around the Mulenge mountains since the late 18th Century is at the heart of the conflict in eastern Zaire.
For Rwanda, the removal of Hutu refugee camps as far from its natural borders as possible is of paramount importance. The latest war in Zaire has achieved that objective.
